composition: Binary Fe-Al alloy with a nominal Al content of 17 at.%; ICP analysis gives a real Al content of 16.6-17.0 at.% (8.8-9.0 wt.-%). The balance is Fe of 99.99% purity (zone-melting purified to minimise impurities), alloyed with Al of 99.999% purity. Impurity contents are low and unavoidable: C <20-70 wt.ppm, Si 60-110 wt.ppm, As <50 wt.ppm and Ni <90 wt.ppm. The Al addition is designed to provide solid-solution hardening, reduced density and oxidation/high-temperature corrosion resistance typical of iron-rich Fe-Al alloys.
conclusions: As a member of the polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al series (0-18 at.% Al), Fe-17%Al confirms that the room-temperature yield stress increases linearly with Al content up to 18 at.% as described by Suzuki's solid-solution hardening theory, with the present polycrystalline as-cast hardening coefficient (~2.2 GPa) notably exceeding literature values for monocrystals (~1 GPa) and for earlier polycrystals (~1.8 GPa). Correspondingly, ductility (elongation before necking and fracture strain) decreases with increasing Al content: the alloy remains ductile at room temperature but undergoes brittle fracture without necking at -100 °C, where deformation twinning also sets in (above 14 at.% Al). The study concludes that low-temperature stress-strain behaviour is controlled primarily by Al solid-solution hardening and quenched-in excess vacancies, with only minor effects of short-range ordering; twinning arises from insufficient dislocation mobility and becomes more pronounced the lower the temperature and the higher the Al content. These results support the development of high-strength, low-density Fe-Al structural materials and quantify the strength-ductility trade-off that must be managed at higher Al contents.
mechanisms: Solid-solution hardening: dissolved Al in the bcc Fe lattice raises the yield stress linearly with Al content up to 18 at.% according to Suzuki's theory of solid-solution hardening for bcc alloys; the polycrystalline as-cast series yields a hardening coefficient of ~2.2 GPa, higher than ~1 GPa reported for Fe-Al monocrystals (2-6% Al) and ~1.8 GPa reported by Morgand et al. for polycrystals at 100 °C, a contrast attributed to differences in alloy preparation (as-cast polycrystals vs monocrystals annealed 900 °C/24 h) and to slip mode (multiple slip in polycrystals vs single slip in monocrystals).

Reduced dislocation mobility with increasing Al content: TEM of polycrystalline Fe-Al shows that distinct cell formation, which requires sufficient dislocation mobility, occurs after deformation only in the furnace-cooled Fe-12%Al alloy and not at higher Al contents; the progressively lower dislocation mobility with increasing Al content is the cause of the decreasing fracture strain (ductility loss), and this effect is enhanced by quenched-in excess vacancies.

Low-temperature deformation twinning: a reduced mobility of screw dislocations is a prerequisite for twin formation in bcc crystals and can be achieved by substitutional alloying; because the number of sufficiently mobile dislocations decreases with increasing Al content and decreasing temperature, deformation twinning occurs the more readily the lower the temperature and the higher the Al content — in Fe-17%Al this produces large load drops (with audible clicks) and metallographic evidence of twins at -100 °C, while at room temperature twinning is seen only at 18 at.% Al.

Ductile-to-brittle transition: the fracture strain parallels the elongation before necking up to about 15 at.% Al at room temperature and about 12 at.% Al at -100 °C, then drops steeply; the transition from ductile fracture with necking to brittle fracture without necking occurs at 15-18 at.% Al at room temperature and at 12-14 at.% Al at -100 °C, so the 17 at.% as-cast alloy is ductile at room temperature but brittle at -100 °C.

Excess-vacancy hardening context: quenching from high temperature (e.g. 1100 °C) traps thermal excess vacancies that are immobile at low temperature and act as effective obstacles to dislocation motion, contributing to hardening and embrittlement; such vacancies heal out only slowly on annealing between 300 and 400 °C, consistent with the observation that even 14 days at 300 °C may not fully eliminate them.

Short-range ordering has no major impact on the deformation behaviour: although short-range ordering in Fe-Al (13-18 at.% Al) is controlled by heat treatments below 600 °C and is nearly suppressed by quenching from 1100 °C, microhardness and stress-strain data vary only by about 5-10%, so only heat treatments above 600 °C significantly affect the mechanical behaviour.

Low-temperature yield-stress drops observed for low-Al as-cast alloys (Fe-4%Al and Fe-6%Al at -100 °C) are attributed to the interaction of mobile dislocations with vacancies, rather than to the B2/D03 dislocation configurations that explain yield drops in higher-Al ordered alloys.
microstructure: As-cast polycrystalline Fe-17%Al consists of a single-phase disordered bcc Fe-Al solid solution with a coarse grain structure, grain sizes on the order of 1 mm. The as-cast alloy contains no second phases: fine thin plate-like or rod-like precipitates (identified by SEM/EDX as carbides, consistent with the carbon content) appear on grain boundaries only after slow furnace cooling from 1100 °C or prolonged annealing (e.g. 14 days at 320 °C), so they are absent in the as-cast state. No crystallographic texture is reported.
processing: The alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting in Al2O3 crucibles from zone-melting-purified Fe (99.99%) and Al (99.999%), followed by solidification in Cu moulds to give rods usually 18 mm in diameter; the studied material was used directly in the as-cast condition, i.e. without any subsequent heat treatment. Compression specimens of 5 × 5 × 10 mm3 were cut by electrostatic discharge machining, mechanically polished with surfaces cleansed by grinding, and cleaned by ultrasound in acetone. Metallographic specimens were etched with an alcoholic 10% nitric acid solution to reveal grain boundaries and precipitates.
properties: Compression yield stress (0.2% proof stress) at room temperature was measured at 10^-2 s^-1 and 10^-4 s^-1; for the polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al series the yield stress rises linearly with Al content up to 18 at.%, with interpolated straight lines indicating increases of 21 MPa per unit% at the higher rate and 23 MPa per unit% at the lower rate (usually two specimens per alloy, data differing by at most 3%). In tension (rate between 10^-4 and 10^-2 s^-1, cylindrical specimens per DIN 50125) the tensile yield stress equals the compressive yield stress at the same rate and temperature, and the ultimate tensile strength parallels the yield stress. At -100 °C the Fe-17%Al curve reaches ~500-550 MPa and then shows abrupt load drops below ~12% strain; yield stress and UTS at -100 °C are about 80 MPa higher than at room temperature. At room temperature the alloy fractures ductilely (brittle fracture without necking only occurs at 18 at.% Al), whereas at -100 °C it fractures brittle without prior necking (brittle fracture at -100 °C sets in above 13 at.% Al). Deformation twinning occurs at -100 °C for Al contents above 14 at.% and therefore in this alloy. Characterization techniques applied to the sample and series include optical microscopy (alcoholic 10% nitric acid etching), ICP analysis, SEM with EDX (fracture surfaces, precipitate analysis), compression testing and tensile testing; TEM was used on related polycrystals to study dislocation substructures.
summary: Polycrystalline binary Fe-Al alloy with a nominal 17 at.% Al content, produced by vacuum induction melting and solidification in a Cu mould and studied in the as-cast condition (no subsequent heat treatment). It exhibits a coarse (~1 mm) single-phase disordered bcc Fe-Al solid-solution structure with no second phases, and serves as one member of the 0-18 at.% Al polycrystalline as-cast series used to clarify how Al solid-solution hardening, reduced dislocation mobility and deformation twinning control strength and ductility at room temperature and at -100 °C.
unmapped: For the polycrystalline as-cast Fe-Al series including Fe-17%Al, the tensile yield stress was found to equal the compressive yield stress at the same rate and temperature, the ultimate tensile strength parallels the yield stress, and at -100 °C both yield stress and UTS are higher than at room temperature by about 80 MPa.

Deformation twinning at -100 °C occurs for Al contents above 14 at.% in all specimens, so Fe-17%Al twins at -100 °C; the corresponding stress for initiating deformation twinning is plotted as a function of Al content at -100 °C.

The alloy belongs to a broader study of binary Fe-Al alloys (4-18 at.% Al) prepared at low unavoidable impurity levels in particular <100 wt.ppm C, in contrast to earlier Fe-Al studies that contained comparatively high carbon (300-600 wt.ppm); monocrystals in the same study were grown by the Bridgman method, but this sample is polycrystalline as-cast.
